title: Structure and Stagecraft
description: Eight-scene structure, dual settings, domestic realism, Obeah and Pinnock's stagecraft choices.
content_html:
Eight Scenes: The Play's Structure

Leave Taking is structured as eight scenes, not two formally titled acts. This is how it appears in the published Nick Hern Books text and how it is organised in performance. In analysis and exam responses, you should refer to 'Scene 1', 'Scene 7' and so on, rather than 'Act 1' or 'Act 2', to be precise about the text you are studying. There is a structural shift roughly in the middle of the play — the first four scenes establishing tension, the second four escalating into crisis and resolution — but this is a structural pattern, not a formal act division.

The pacing across the eight scenes is deliberate: Scenes 1–5 are slower, domestic, built around everyday tensions — arguments about respectability, education, money, the letter from Jamaica. Scenes 6–8 accelerate as crises converge — Del at Mai's, Enid searching for her, Brod's revelation, and the final reconciliation. This structural contrast mirrors the family's experience: years of quiet suppression followed by a crisis that forces everything into the open.

Key Fact

Pinnock's choice to build the early scenes around domestic routine before cracking it open in the later scenes reflects the real experience of immigrant families: cultural conflict often simmers beneath the surface of ordinary life for years before a crisis forces it into the open. The structure of the play is part of Pinnock's argument.

Dual Settings: Two Physical Spaces

Leave Taking has two distinct physical settings. Enid's North London living room appears in Scenes 2–5: the domestic English space, defined by routine, respectability and suppression. Mai's Deptford bedsit appears in Scenes 1, 6, 7 and 8: the Caribbean spiritual space, associated with Obeah, cultural roots and healing. Crucially, the play opens at Mai's bedsit (Scene 1) and ends there (Scene 8). This means the Caribbean spiritual world frames the entire action — it is where the story begins and where it is resolved.

Pinnock's staging of two physical settings is itself a structural statement. Enid's home is the space she controls; Mai's bedsit is the space Enid cannot control. Del gravitates from one to the other across the play. The final resolution can only happen at Mai's — not in Enid's living room. This tells us something about what the play argues: the family cannot heal in the space built on suppression; they must go to the space built on honesty.

Leave Taking is written in a domestic realist style for much of its length. The dialogue sounds like real speech: overlapping, interrupted, emotionally loaded. Characters argue about tea, homework, clothes and money — the fabric of ordinary domestic life. Pinnock uses this realism to show that the play's grand themes (identity, belonging, cultural displacement) are not abstract but lived in every meal, every conversation, every loaded silence. The domestic setting is not a backdrop — it is where culture is fought over.

Obeah: Breaking Realism

While the play is predominantly naturalistic, Mai's Obeah practice introduces a spiritual dimension that complicates the realism. When Mai performs rituals, reads palms or speaks of the spirit world, the language becomes more poetic and the atmosphere more charged. Pinnock does not present Obeah as superstition to be mocked; she treats it as a legitimate cultural practice with real power and real wisdom.

This structural tension between domestic realism and the spirit world is itself thematic. Enid has tried to live entirely in the 'rational' English world, rejecting Caribbean spirituality. Mai's presence reintroduces the spiritual dimension Enid suppressed. The play's hybrid form — realism interrupted by spirituality — mirrors the dual cultural identity the characters are navigating. You cannot fully separate the two registers any more than the characters can fully separate their two cultural identities.

Pinnock builds dramatic tension through gradual revelation. Enid's backstory — the abusive marriage, the estrangement from her mother, the shame about her Jamaican roots — is revealed in pieces across the play rather than in a single dramatic disclosure. Del's pregnancy is also revealed gradually. This technique of foreshadowing engages the audience as active interpreters, rewarding close attention to dialogue and behaviour. In Scene 1 we already know something is wrong before we understand exactly what.

The parallel crises of Del's pregnancy and Viv's exam rebellion create structural echoes: both daughters find their own way of refusing the identity Enid designed for them. This parallelism deepens the play's exploration of intergenerational patterns — the daughters are not simply rebelling but finding themselves.

For AQA Paper 2, discussing Pinnock's structural and staging choices is essential AO2 material. The eight-scene structure, the two physical settings, domestic realism, the hybrid incorporation of Obeah, and the technique of gradual revelation are all deliberate choices that shape meaning. Always explain why Pinnock makes these choices, not just that she does.

Key Fact

Understanding the playwright's specific choices — structure, language, staging and context — is essential for top-band analysis. Make sure you can discuss how form and content work together to create meaning for the audience.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the unseen writer use setting to explore ideas about belonging. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's two physical settings: Enid's living room (assimilation, suppression) and Mai's Deptford bedsit (Caribbean spiritual space, healing). The structural significance of the play opening and closing at Mai's bedsit. Compares with the unseen writer's approach. AO3 integrated.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison with some analysis of setting as technique.

Lower band (1–8): Describes settings rather than analysing their dramatic function.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Pinnock uses the play's structure to develop her themes in Leave Taking. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses the eight-scene structure. Discusses: early scenes establishing suppression through domestic routine; later scenes accelerating into crisis (Del at Mai's, Brod's revelation, the final confrontation). The play's opening and closing at Mai's bedsit as structural statement. Links to immigrant experience.

Mid band (9–16): Clear discussion of structure with some analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description of what happens.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock use domestic realism in Leave Taking? Why does she choose this dramatic form? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses domestic realism as a deliberate choice: everyday settings ground grand themes in lived experience. Discusses: overlapping dialogue, arguments about domestic life (food, clothes, money) as cultural battlegrounds. Contrasts with Obeah scenes. Links to Pinnock's purpose of centering Caribbean-British women's daily lives.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis with some evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Limited engagement with dramatic form.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the unseen writer blend realism with a non-realistic element. Consider language and dramatic technique. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's hybrid form — domestic realism interrupted by Obeah's spiritual dimension. Discusses how this mirrors the characters' dual cultural identity. Compares with the unseen writer's technique. AO3 integrated.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison with some analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Pinnock uses the two settings of Leave Taking to convey her themes. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses both settings as thematically loaded spaces. Enid's living room: assimilation, English respectability, suppression. Mai's Deptford bedsit: Caribbean spiritual tradition, healing, honesty. The structural significance of the play opening and closing at Mai's. The resolution happening at Mai's, not Enid's home — what this argues about where healing is possible.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description of settings.

practice_questions.text: 'The domestic setting in Leave Taking is not just a backdrop — it is where cultural identity is fought over.' How far do you agree? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Evaluative response. Agrees: arguments about food, language, education, clothes all carry cultural weight in Enid's living room. May consider how Mai's bedsit is equally a cultural space — but a different one. Discusses the play's two physical settings as representing two competing cultural identities. Nuanced conclusion.

Mid band (9–16): Clear argument with evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Simple agreement.

knowledge_checks.q: How many scenes does Leave Taking have in the published text?
Which scenes take place at Mai's Deptford bedsit?
The play's _____ form — realism interrupted by Obeah's spiritual dimension — mirrors the characters' dual cultural identity.
Pinnock builds dramatic tension through gradual _____ — revealing Enid's backstory in pieces rather than a single disclosure.
Match each setting to what it represents thematically:
right: English respectability, assimilation, suppression — the space Enid controls
Caribbean spiritual tradition, healing, honesty — the space that frames the whole play

flashcard_questions.q: How is Leave Taking structured in the published text?
flashcard_questions.a: Eight scenes — not two formal acts. References in analysis should use scene numbers.

flashcard_questions.q: Which scenes take place at Enid's living room, and which at Mai's bedsit?
flashcard_questions.a: Enid's living room: Scenes 2–5. Mai's Deptford bedsit: Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it structurally significant that the play opens and closes at Mai's bedsit?
flashcard_questions.a: The Caribbean spiritual space frames the entire action — it is where the story begins and where it is resolved.
A dramatic style representing everyday life realistically through believable dialogue and everyday settings.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Pinnock use domestic realism?
flashcard_questions.a: To show that themes of identity, belonging and displacement are lived in every meal and conversation — not abstract ideas.
A Caribbean system of folk magic, healing and spiritual practice rooted in West African traditions.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Pinnock treat Obeah in the play?
flashcard_questions.a: As a legitimate cultural practice with real power and wisdom — not as superstition to be mocked.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the play's hybrid form?
flashcard_questions.a: Domestic realism interrupted by Mai's spiritual register — mirroring the characters' dual cultural identity.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Pinnock use foreshadowing in the play?
flashcard_questions.a: Hints in Scene 1 (Enid's worry about Del, the letter from Jamaica) reward active audience attention before later revelations.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can the resolution only happen at Mai's bedsit rather than Enid's home?
flashcard_questions.a: Enid's home is built on suppression — healing requires the honest space that Mai's bedsit represents.

glossary_terms.definition: A dramatic style representing everyday life realistically, with believable dialogue and settings.
A Caribbean system of folk magic, healing and spiritual practice rooted in West African traditions.
The combination of realistic and non-realistic elements within a single work — domestic realism interrupted by spirituality in Leave Taking.
Hints or clues planted early in a text that point towards later revelations.
Two contrasting physical spaces representing different values: Enid's living room (English respectability) and Mai's Deptford bedsit (Caribbean spiritual tradition).
The way a playwright's choice of structure itself communicates thematic meaning.

exam_tip_html: When writing about Structure and Stagecraft, focus your analysis on the specific dramatic and structural choices the playwright makes. Examiners reward responses that connect language details to wider themes, and that show understanding of the social and historical context in which the play was written. Avoid retelling the plot — instead, explain the effect of specific techniques on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • This lesson has covered the key ideas and dramatic techniques relevant to Structure and Stagecraft. Make sure you can discuss specific examples from the text, link techniques to themes, and embed relevant context in your analysis.
